notes.front: In the Evidence-Based Management Guide, what is a feature?
notes.back: A distinguishing characteristic of a product, which the Guide treats alongside other requirements.
notes.explanation: The Guide notes that organisations can spend a lot of money implementing features and other requirements.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Organizations can spend a lot of money implementing features (distinguishing characteristics) and other requirements in products
notes.example: Like a car’s heated seats: one characteristic that sets the model apart, whether or not buyers care about it.

notes.front: How does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say organisations must tackle complex problems?
notes.back: By experimenting toward larger goals in small steps, comparing each result with the desired outcome and adapting the next step.
notes.explanation: Complex problems do not have easy solutions, so each step is treated as an experiment to learn from.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Complex problems don't have easy solutions. In order to solve them, organizations must experiment by defining, working toward, and achieving larger goals in small steps. Each step involves comparing the actual result of the experiment with its desired outcome, and adapting the next step based accordingly

notes.front: What role does the Evidence-Based Management Guide give inputs in experiments?
notes.back: They set constraints, such as a limit on how much a team may spend to test an improvement idea.
notes.explanation: Inputs are what the organisation spends money on; their amount has no correlation with customer value, yet they can still bound an experiment.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience. Inputs establish constraints on experiments, e.g. an organization may establish limits on how much a team may spend (the input) to test an improvement idea.

notes.front: When starting toward a Strategic Goal, why does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say you will probably need to understand your own capability for delivering value?
notes.back: So that you can set realistic short and medium term goals.
notes.explanation: Capability here means how fast you can make improvements in the value your customers will experience.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You will probably also need to understand your own capability for delivering value, i.e. how fast you are able to make improvements in the value that your customers will experience, so that you can set realistic short and medium term goals.

notes.front: Not all changes improve results; some changes actually {{c1::make things worse}}.
notes.back: make things worse
notes.explanation: The Inspect step asks whether the change improved results, based on the measurements made.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Inspecting your results. Did the change you made improve your results based on the measurements you have made? Not all changes do; some changes actually make things worse.

notes.front: After an experiment, which adaptation question checks the near-term target the experiment aimed at?
notes.back: Was the Immediate Tactical Goal the right goal?
notes.explanation: It questions the target itself, not only the tactics used to reach it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Was the Immediate Tactical Goal the right goal?

notes.front: Which of the Guide’s adaptation questions looks beyond the Immediate Tactical Goal to the longer-range goals?
notes.back: Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant, or do they need to be adapted?
notes.explanation: Relevance is the test: a longer-range goal can stop being worth pursuing.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant or do they need to be adapted?

notes.front: You missed an Immediate Tactical Goal that you still think is important. Which adaptation question does the Guide suggest?
notes.back: How might you do better next time?
notes.explanation: The question applies only when the missed goal still matters; otherwise the goal itself is in question.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you failed to achieve the Immediate Tactical Goal but you think it is still important to achieve, how might you do better next time?

notes.front: Among the Guide’s examples for adapting goals, what do you need to do after achieving your Intermediate or Strategic Goals?
notes.back: Formulate new goals.
notes.explanation: Reaching a goal does not end adaptation; the set of goals is renewed.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you achieved your Intermediate or Strategic Goals you will need to formulate new goals.

notes.front: Besides what you learn from experiments, what else can change your goals, according to the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: Outside events; your tactics for reaching the goals may then need to be reconsidered and revised.
notes.explanation: Goals are not fixed once set; the world around the product moves too.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Goals can change because of outside events, and your tactics to reach your goals may need to be reconsidered and revised

notes.front: Beliefs in what is valuable are merely {{c1::assumptions}} until they are validated by customers.
notes.back: assumptions
notes.explanation: Organisations can spend a lot on features only to find customers do not share their opinion of the value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: only to find that customers don’t share the company’s opinion on their value; beliefs in what is valuable are merely assumptions until they are validated by customers.

notes.front: Forming hypotheses, measuring results and adapting goals are already implicit in an agile approach. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say it adds?
notes.back: Making this work explicit and transparent.
notes.explanation: The Guide agrees the work is already implicit in an agile approach; its addition is to the organisational improvement process.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Explicitly forming hypotheses, measuring results, and inspecting and adapting goals based on those results are implicit parts of an agile approach. Making this work explicit and transparent is what EBM adds to the organizational improvement process.

notes.front: You achieve your Immediate Tactical Goal. What is the next step, according to the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: Form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that takes you closer to your Intermediate Goal, and keep devising experiments toward it.
notes.explanation: Each Immediate Tactical Goal is one step on the path to the Intermediate Goal, not an end in itself.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: If you succeed in achieving your Immediate Tactical Goal, congratulations! Your next step will be to form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that, when achieved, will take you closer to your Intermediate Goal. Continue devising experiments, or things you can try, to achieve that goal.

notes.front: You achieve an Intermediate Goal. Which new goals does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say you need to form?
notes.back: A new Intermediate Goal and a new Immediate Tactical Goal.
notes.explanation: The new Intermediate Goal moves you closer to the Strategic Goal, and the new Immediate Tactical Goal gives a nearer target to work toward.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Now you’ll need to form a new Intermediate Goal that, when you achieve it, will move you closer to your Strategic Goal. You’ll also need to form a new Immediate Tactical Goal to provide you with a nearer target to work toward.

notes.front: A goal may turn out to be no longer relevant, or to need refining, and this can happen to goals at {{c1::any level}}.
notes.back: any level
notes.explanation: The Guide says goals sometimes need adjusting, whether strategic, intermediate or immediate.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Sometimes you’ll find that your goals need adjusting. You might discover that a goal is no longer relevant, or that it needs to be refined. This can happen to your goals at any level.

notes.front: A Product Owner’s Strategic Goal is to halve how long patients wait for a doctor’s appointment across a region. A director wants a two-year plan with every feature fixed now. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide suggest instead?
notes.back: C) Work toward it in small steps, comparing each result with the desired outcome.
notes.choices:
A) Fix the plan now, then measure only at the end
B) Wait until every requirement is known before starting
C) Work toward it in small steps, comparing each result with the desired outcome
D) Double the team so the plan finishes sooner
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: a complex problem has no easy, fully known solution to plan up front. D: adding inputs does not correlate with the value customers experience.
notes.explanation: Complex problems have no easy solutions, so the Guide has organisations experiment in small steps.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Complex problems don't have easy solutions. In order to solve them, organizations must experiment by defining, working toward, and achieving larger goals in small steps. Each step involves comparing the actual result of the experiment with its desired outcome, and adapting the next step based accordingly

notes.front: After a release, the team compares the actual result with the outcome it wanted and finds a gap. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say comes next?
notes.back: D) Adapt the next step based on that comparison.
notes.choices:
A) Repeat the same step unchanged
B) Stop experimenting until the gap closes itself
C) Report the release as a success, since it shipped
D) Adapt the next step based on that comparison
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: the Guide has each step adapt the next one. C: shipping is an output; the comparison was with the desired outcome.
notes.explanation: Each small step involves comparing the result with the desired outcome and adapting the next step accordingly.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “EBM Helps Organizations Achieve Their Goals in a Complex World”, p. 3
notes.evidence: Complex problems don't have easy solutions. In order to solve them, organizations must experiment by defining, working toward, and achieving larger goals in small steps. Each step involves comparing the actual result of the experiment with its desired outcome, and adapting the next step based accordingly

notes.front: The board offers to double a product’s budget so that it will deliver twice the value to customers. What should the Product Owner point out?
notes.back: B) Inputs have no correlation with the value customers experience.
notes.choices:
A) Double the budget should double the value
B) Inputs have no correlation with the value customers experience
C) Budget is an impact the board can count
D) Budget is an output, so it should be measured
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is exactly the correlation the Guide denies. D: budget is an input, not an output. C: impacts are results such as revenue, not money spent.
notes.explanation: Spending is an input: necessary to produce value, but no guide to how much value customers get.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience.

notes.front: A status report offers hours worked, money spent and team size as proof that the product is delivering value. What is wrong with it?
notes.back: A) It measures inputs and activities, which say nothing about the value customers experience.
notes.choices:
A) It measures inputs and activities, which say nothing about the value customers experience
B) Nothing: effort is a good measure of value
C) It should report team size first
D) It should include the number of meetings held
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: effort and size are inputs and activities. D: meetings are activities too, adding nothing about value.
notes.explanation: Money spent is an input, and the Guide says input amounts have no correlation with customer value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs. These are things that the organization spends money on. While necessary to produce value, there is no correlation between the amount of input and the value that customers experience.

notes.front: Finance caps the spend for testing a new sign-up idea at a fixed amount. How does the Evidence-Based Management Guide see such a cap?
notes.back: D) As an input used to constrain an experiment.
notes.choices:
A) As an impact on investors
B) As an outcome of the experiment
C) As a reason not to run the experiment
D) As an input used to constrain an experiment
notes.choicesExplained: B: outcomes are what customers experience. C: the Guide gives this very kind of limit as a normal constraint. A: impacts are results such as revenue or share price.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s own example of inputs setting constraints is a limit on how much a team may spend to test an idea.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 5
notes.evidence: Inputs establish constraints on experiments, e.g. an organization may establish limits on how much a team may spend (the input) to test an improvement idea.

notes.front: To save costs, a banking app withdraws a cheque-scanning service that many customers relied on. How would the Evidence-Based Management Guide classify the change for those customers?
notes.back: B) A negative outcome.
notes.choices:
A) A positive impact
B) A negative outcome
C) An input saving only
D) A neutral output
notes.choicesExplained: A: an impact is an organisation’s result, and the customers’ side is what is asked. D and C: both ignore the decline the customers experience.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s own example of a negative outcome is a relied-on service that is no longer available.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: can also be negative, as in the case where the value a customer or user experiences declines from previous experiences, for example when a service they previously relied upon is no longer available.

notes.front: A Product Owner retires an export function that many users depended on, and reports “no change in outcomes” because nothing new was added. Is she right?
notes.back: C) No: outcomes can be negative when users lose something they relied on.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: outcomes only change when something is added
B) Yes: removing things affects outputs only
C) No: outcomes can be negative when users lose something they relied on
D) No: removal is an input, so it must be measured
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Guide says outcomes can decline. D: removing a function is not something the organisation spends money on.
notes.explanation: Outcomes are measured against the customer’s previous experience, which can get worse.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: can also be negative, as in the case where the value a customer or user experiences declines from previous experiences, for example when a service they previously relied upon is no longer available.

notes.front: A product dashboard shows items completed, releases shipped and meetings held. A stakeholder asks what it cannot tell them. What is the best answer?
notes.back: C) What customers actually experience as a result.
notes.choices:
A) How many releases were shipped
B) How busy the team was
C) What customers actually experience as a result
D) How many meetings took place
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: the dashboard already shows these, which are outputs and activities, the easy things to measure.
notes.explanation: Activities and outputs are easy to measure, while outcomes are hard, and this dashboard shows only the easy kind.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: The problem most organizations face, which is often reflected in the things they measure, is that measuring activities and outputs is easy, while measuring outcomes is difficult. Organizations may gather a lot of data with insufficient information about their ability to deliver value.

notes.front: A team shipped 40 features this quarter against 20 last quarter. A manager says customers must be twice as happy. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say?
notes.back: B) Delivering more features does not necessarily improve customer experiences.
notes.choices:
A) Twice the features means twice the value
B) Delivering more features does not necessarily improve customer experiences
C) Customer happiness follows the number of releases
D) Features are outcomes, so the claim is proven
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the Guide denies that more output necessarily improves outcomes. D: features are outputs, not outcomes.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives this very case, more features, as output that need not lead to better outcomes.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: For example, working more hours (activities) and delivering more features (outputs) does not necessarily lead to improved customer experiences (outcomes).

notes.front: To hit a profit target, a vice-president proposes cutting testing so that the product costs less to build. Profit would rise this year. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide warn?
notes.back: D) Improving impacts without improving customer outcomes usually harms the organisation.
notes.choices:
A) Profit is an outcome, so this improves value
B) Nothing, as long as revenue also rises
C) Testing is an input, so cutting it is always safe
D) Improving impacts without improving customer outcomes usually harms the organisation
notes.choicesExplained: A: profit is an impact, not a customer outcome. B: revenue is an impact too. C: the Guide gives reducing quality to improve profit as a harmful example.
notes.explanation: The Guide names reducing product quality to improve profitability as its example of harmful impact-chasing.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While it is possible for organizations to improve impacts without improving customer outcomes, doing so usually harms the organization, such as when it reduces product quality to improve profitability, or when it sells products below cost to increase revenue and market share but harms profitability.

notes.front: The sales team wants to price the product below cost to grab market share quickly. Market share would rise. How should the Product Owner weigh this, using the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: D) Impacts gained without better customer outcomes usually harm the organisation, as below-cost selling harms profit.
notes.choices:
A) Market share is an impact, so any rise is sustainable
B) Pricing is not a Product Owner concern at all
C) Market share is an outcome, so it proves customer value
D) Impacts gained without better customer outcomes usually harm the organisation, as below-cost selling harms profit
notes.choicesExplained: A: impacts are only sustainable through improved customer outcomes. C: market share is an impact. B: the Product Owner is accountable for maximising the product’s value, which this affects.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s second harmful example is selling below cost to raise revenue and market share while harming profitability.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Understanding What is Valuable”, p. 6
notes.evidence: While it is possible for organizations to improve impacts without improving customer outcomes, doing so usually harms the organization, such as when it reduces product quality to improve profitability, or when it sells products below cost to increase revenue and market share but harms profitability.

notes.front: A new Product Owner sets a goal to halve checkout time within two weeks, without knowing how fast the team can deliver improvements. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide suggest she understand first?
notes.back: C) The organisation’s own capability for delivering value.
notes.choices:
A) The size of next year’s budget
B) Only the competitors’ checkout times
C) The organisation’s own capability for delivering value
D) Nothing: ambitious goals motivate the team
notes.choicesExplained: B and A: neither tells her how fast her own team can improve. D: the Guide ties realistic short and medium term goals to knowing that capability.
notes.explanation: Knowing how fast you can make improvements is what makes short and medium term goals realistic.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You will probably also need to understand your own capability for delivering value, i.e. how fast you are able to make improvements in the value that your customers will experience, so that you can set realistic short and medium term goals.

notes.front: A Product Owner knows what her customers experience today and what they would like in future. What else does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say she will probably need before setting realistic goals?
notes.back: D) How fast her organisation can improve the value customers experience.
notes.choices:
A) A fixed release date
B) A larger budget
C) A list of every feature
D) How fast her organisation can improve the value customers experience
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: none of these describes the organisation’s capability to deliver value, which the Guide names.
notes.explanation: Understanding the current state covers both the customers’ experience and your own capability to improve it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: You will probably also need to understand your own capability for delivering value, i.e. how fast you are able to make improvements in the value that your customers will experience, so that you can set realistic short and medium term goals.

notes.front: A team’s hypothesis reads: “A simpler sign-up form will help.” Nothing else is written down. What is missing before the experiment runs?
notes.back: C) A decision on how measurement will show whether it succeeded.
notes.choices:
A) Approval from every stakeholder
B) A larger design team
C) A decision on how measurement will show whether it succeeded
D) A full specification of the form
notes.choicesExplained: B, A and D: none is part of forming the hypothesis in the Guide; deciding how success will be measured is.
notes.explanation: Without an agreed measure, the Inspect step has nothing to judge the result against.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Forming a hypothesis for improvement. Based on experience, form an idea of something you think will help you move toward your Immediate Tactical Goal, and decide how you will know whether this experiment succeeded based on measurement.

notes.front: Which hypothesis is ready to run as an experiment under the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: D) “Showing delivery times at checkout will raise completed orders by a tenth within a month”.
notes.choices:
A) “Customers will like the new menu”
B) “The redesign is the right thing to do”
C) “Stakeholders asked for dark mode, so we will build it”
D) “Showing delivery times at checkout will raise completed orders by a tenth within a month”
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: none says how measurement would show success, which the Guide asks you to decide when forming the hypothesis.
notes.explanation: Only this one states the change and how its success will be known.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 6
notes.evidence: Forming a hypothesis for improvement. Based on experience, form an idea of something you think will help you move toward your Immediate Tactical Goal, and decide how you will know whether this experiment succeeded based on measurement.

notes.front: After a checkout redesign, the share of completed purchases drops. The designer says the change must be kept because “changes are improvements”. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say?
notes.back: A) Not all changes improve results; some make things worse.
notes.choices:
A) Not all changes improve results; some make things worse
B) Keep it: every change improves results in time
C) Stop measuring checkout completion
D) Blame the Developers for the drop
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says the opposite. C: the measurement is what showed the problem. D: the Guide’s Inspect step is about results, not blame.
notes.explanation: Inspecting results against measurements is how you find out whether a change helped.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Inspecting your results. Did the change you made improve your results based on the measurements you have made? Not all changes do; some changes actually make things worse.

notes.front: A stakeholder wants the team to skip checking the results of a change because it “obviously” helps. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: D) Inspect the results against the measures, since some changes make things worse.
notes.choices:
A) Skip it: obvious changes need no checking
B) Check only if customers complain
C) Check next year, when data is complete
D) Inspect the results against the measures, since some changes make things worse
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Guide does not exempt obvious changes. C: the loop inspects each experiment’s results, not once a year.
notes.explanation: Not all changes improve results, so the Guide has you inspect the results against your measures rather than assume the change helped.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Inspecting your results. Did the change you made improve your results based on the measurements you have made? Not all changes do; some changes actually make things worse.

notes.front: The team reaches its Immediate Tactical Goal, but a new regulation makes the Intermediate Goal look pointless. Which adaptation question fits best?
notes.back: B) Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant, or do they need adapting?
notes.choices:
A) How might we do better next time?
B) Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant, or do they need adapting?
C) How many features did we ship?
D) Was the Immediate Tactical Goal the right goal?
notes.choicesExplained: A: that is for a missed goal that still matters. D: the doubt here is about the Intermediate Goal. C: that counts output and adapts nothing.
notes.explanation: The doubt is about a longer-range goal’s relevance, which is exactly what this question asks.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Are the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still relevant or do they need to be adapted?

notes.front: The team missed its Immediate Tactical Goal, and everyone agrees it still matters. Which adaptation question fits best?
notes.back: D) If it is still important, how might we do better next time?
notes.choices:
A) Who is to blame?
B) Should we drop all our goals?
C) Was the Strategic Goal ever achievable?
D) If it is still important, how might we do better next time?
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: nothing suggests the longer-range goals are in doubt. A: blame is not one of the Guide’s questions.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this question with a missed goal that is still worth reaching.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: If you failed to achieve the Immediate Tactical Goal but you think it is still important to achieve, how might you do better next time?

notes.front: A competitor launches a free version of a similar product, making the team’s current tactics pointless. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say?
notes.back: A) Goals can change because of outside events, and tactics may need revising.
notes.choices:
A) Goals can change because of outside events, and tactics may need revising
B) Only the Strategic Goal can change
C) Goals are fixed once agreed and must not change
D) Ignore competitors and keep going
notes.choicesExplained: C and B: the Guide says goals at any level can change. D: the Guide names outside events as a reason to reconsider tactics.
notes.explanation: Outside events, not only your own experiments, can change goals and the tactics for reaching them.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Making Progress Toward Goals in a Series of Small Steps”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Goals can change because of outside events, and your tactics to reach your goals may need to be reconsidered and revised

notes.front: The chief executive insists a feature is valuable because everyone in head office loves it. How should the Product Owner treat that belief?
notes.back: B) As an assumption until customers validate it.
notes.choices:
A) As proven, since leadership agrees
B) As an assumption until customers validate it
C) As a requirement that needs no testing
D) As an outcome already achieved
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: agreement inside the company is not validation by customers. D: an outcome is what customers experience, not what staff believe.
notes.explanation: Beliefs about value are merely assumptions until customers validate them.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: only to find that customers don’t share the company’s opinion on their value; beliefs in what is valuable are merely assumptions until they are validated by customers.

notes.front: A Product Owner receives thirty requirements from stakeholders, each marked “must have”. How does the Evidence-Based Management Guide suggest she treat them?
notes.back: A) As hypotheses about value to be tested.
notes.choices:
A) As hypotheses about value to be tested
B) As commitments to build in full
C) As outputs to count toward value
D) As inputs with fixed costs
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says every requirement is really a hypothesis. C: counting outputs does not show value. D: a requirement is not something the organisation spends money on.
notes.explanation: Every feature and requirement represents a hypothesis about value, which experiments can test.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Every feature and every requirement really represents a hypothesis about value. One of the goals of an empirical approach is to make these hypotheses explicit and to consciously design experiments that explicitly test the value of the features and requirements.

notes.front: A Product Owner wants to know whether customers would pay for premium reports. The current plan is six months of full development. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide suggest?
notes.back: D) Build enough to validate the critical assumptions about its value.
notes.choices:
A) Build it all, then ask customers
B) Decide from stakeholders’ opinions, without testing
C) Build twice as fast with more people
D) Build enough to validate the critical assumptions about its value
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the entire feature need not be built to test its value. B: beliefs about value are merely assumptions until customers validate them. C: more inputs do not answer the value question.
notes.explanation: A partial build can prove or disprove the value long before the full build would.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: The team wonders whether customers want voice ordering. Which approach best fits the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: A) Build a small slice that tests whether customers use it.
notes.choices:
A) Build a small slice that tests whether customers use it
B) Ask the chief executive to decide
C) Build every voice command before release
D) Wait until a competitor builds it
notes.choicesExplained: C: the entire feature need not be built to test its value. B: an executive’s belief is still an assumption. D: waiting tests nothing.
notes.explanation: Building enough to validate the critical assumptions tests the value without the full cost.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: A small first slice of a new feature showed customers do not value it. A stakeholder wants the rest built anyway “since we started”. What should the Product Owner say?
notes.back: A) The slice disproved its value, which is what the partial build was for.
notes.choices:
A) The slice disproved its value, which is what the partial build was for
B) Finish it: half-built features are waste
C) Build the rest, then test again
D) Hide the results and move on
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: building the rest spends more on a feature already shown to lack value. D: the result is evidence, and hiding it helps no one decide.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s point of building enough is to prove or disprove the value, and this build disproved it.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: A manager says: “We are agile, so we already test ideas and adapt. Evidence-Based Management adds nothing.” What does the Guide say it adds?
notes.back: B) Making hypotheses, measures and adaptation explicit and transparent.
notes.choices:
A) A fixed set of measures every organisation must use
B) Making hypotheses, measures and adaptation explicit and transparent
C) A replacement for Scrum
D) A yearly planning cycle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide’s example measures are examples, not a fixed set. C and D: the Guide claims neither.
notes.explanation: The Guide agrees the work is implicit in an agile approach and says making it explicit is its contribution.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Explicitly forming hypotheses, measuring results, and inspecting and adapting goals based on those results are implicit parts of an agile approach. Making this work explicit and transparent is what EBM adds to the organizational improvement process.

notes.front: A Product Owner keeps her hypotheses and success measures in her head, so stakeholders cannot see why items are ordered as they are. What would Evidence-Based Management add here?
notes.back: C) Making the hypotheses and measures explicit and transparent.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: hypotheses are private to the Product Owner
B) A larger backlog
C) Making the hypotheses and measures explicit and transparent
D) A vote by stakeholders on each item
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide’s contribution is exactly to make this work explicit. B and D: neither makes the hypotheses visible.
notes.explanation: Visible hypotheses and measures let others inspect the reasoning behind the order.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Explicitly forming hypotheses, measuring results, and inspecting and adapting goals based on those results are implicit parts of an agile approach. Making this work explicit and transparent is what EBM adds to the organizational improvement process.

notes.front: An experiment missed its Immediate Tactical Goal. A manager wants it left out of the Sprint Review so that stakeholders do not see a “failure”. What fits the Evidence-Based Management Guide?
notes.back: C) Share it: missing the goal is not a bad thing, and the learning shapes new experiments.
notes.choices:
A) Leave it out: failures hurt confidence
B) Show it only if stakeholders ask
C) Share it: missing the goal is not a bad thing, and the learning shapes new experiments
D) Rerun it silently until it works
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: each hides what was learned; the Guide treats the missed goal as a source of learning, not something to hide.
notes.explanation: What you learned from a missed goal helps you devise experiments that may do better.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: And sometimes you’ll fail to reach your Immediate Tactical Goal because your experiment did not produce the results you had expected. This is not a bad thing, and what you learned helps you to devise new experiments that may yield better results.

notes.front: After two experiments miss their targets, a Product Owner proposes giving up on experiments and just building the roadmap. What does the Evidence-Based Management Guide suggest?
notes.back: A) Use what was learned to devise new experiments.
notes.choices:
A) Use what was learned to devise new experiments
B) Give up: two misses prove experiments do not work
C) Hide the misses and continue the roadmap
D) Replace experiments with more features
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Guide says a missed goal is not a bad thing and uses the learning. D: more output does not replace learning about value.
notes.explanation: Each missed target produced learning that the next experiments can use.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: And sometimes you’ll fail to reach your Immediate Tactical Goal because your experiment did not produce the results you had expected. This is not a bad thing, and what you learned helps you to devise new experiments that may yield better results.

notes.front: The team reaches its Immediate Tactical Goal. The Intermediate Goal is not yet reached. What should the Product Owner do next?
notes.back: C) Form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that moves closer to the Intermediate Goal.
notes.choices:
A) Declare the product finished
B) Replace the Strategic Goal
C) Form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that moves closer to the Intermediate Goal
D) Stop experiments until the Intermediate Goal is reached
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the Intermediate and Strategic Goals still stand. D: the Guide says to keep devising experiments toward the new target.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s next step after success is a new, nearer target on the same path.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: If you succeed in achieving your Immediate Tactical Goal, congratulations! Your next step will be to form a new Immediate Tactical Goal that, when achieved, will take you closer to your Intermediate Goal. Continue devising experiments, or things you can try, to achieve that goal.

notes.front: The team reaches its Intermediate Goal. Which goals does the Evidence-Based Management Guide say it needs to form now?
notes.back: C) A new Intermediate Goal and a new Immediate Tactical Goal.
notes.choices:
A) A new Strategic Goal only
B) No new goals until the Strategic Goal is reached
C) A new Intermediate Goal and a new Immediate Tactical Goal
D) A new Immediate Tactical Goal only
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Strategic Goal still stands. B: the team would have no target. D: the Intermediate level also needs a new goal.
notes.explanation: Both levels below the Strategic Goal need a new target once the Intermediate Goal is met.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Now you’ll need to form a new Intermediate Goal that, when you achieve it, will move you closer to your Strategic Goal. You’ll also need to form a new Immediate Tactical Goal to provide you with a nearer target to work toward.

notes.front: Months in, a Product Owner realises the Strategic Goal is worded too vaguely to tell whether progress is being made. May it be refined?
notes.back: D) Yes: goals at any level may need refining.
notes.choices:
A) No: only Immediate Tactical Goals can change
B) No: Strategic Goals are fixed for good
C) Only after the Intermediate Goal is reached
D) Yes: goals at any level may need refining
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: the Guide says the need to adjust or refine can happen to goals at any level, without a waiting rule.
notes.explanation: Goals at every level can turn out irrelevant or in need of refining.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: Sometimes you’ll find that your goals need adjusting. You might discover that a goal is no longer relevant, or that it needs to be refined. This can happen to your goals at any level.
